speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: asked the Prime Minister whether the Government will consider increasing the period during which Government-Paid Paternity Leave may be consumed from within 12 months of childbirth to within 24 months of childbirth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For this reason, we have progressively increased parental leave provisions to support fathers in caring for their children.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is also in line with international practice where parents are typically required to consume maternity and paternity leave within a few months or up to a year after the child's birth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is the practice in many countries, such as Denmark, the United Kingdom (UK) and South Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is a provision under the Tripartite Standard on Unpaid Leave for Unexpected Care Needs, which I must thank the Member Mr Louis Ng for helping to bring about.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Beyond leave provisions, the Government will continue to work with employers to better support parents in managing their work and family responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This includes promoting the adoption of flexible work arrangements and encouraging more family-friendly practices at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am just wondering whether the Ministry is looking into this further, whether we are looking at Denmark, the UK and South Korea, the three countries that the Minister mentioned, what is the take-up rate of paternity leave there and what are they doing that can help increase our take-up of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the default arrangement now is that the fathers have to take their paternity leave within 16 weeks of childbirth and he has to take it in a two-week continuous block.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For any other arrangements, they would need the employers' consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am just wondering whether we can make the default arrangement that the fathers can take it anytime within the 12 months of childbirth and they do not need to take it in a continuous block.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Maybe then, there will be an increase in the number of fathers taking up the paternity leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The figure of 65%, if I recall correctly, is within a certain period of reporting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What happens is that you need the employers to have submitted the claims in order for the true picture to emerge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, usually, fathers have one year after the child's birth to take leave and employers have three months after the fathers take leave to submit the claims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I would take that 65% in context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member asked about the experience in other countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I still recall visiting Denmark, one of the Nordic countries that is very well-known for its family-friendly policies as well as, overall, very strong support for parenthood.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If my memory serves me right, I was myself quite surprised that their paternity leave utilisation was just about 70%, not higher than that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I asked my counterpart to explain to me why this was so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I recall quite distinctly being told that even in a country like Denmark, there are certain sectors where it is just not considered at the workplace to be very acceptable for the man to go on paternity leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is the reason why, even for them, the paternity leave is not closer to 100%.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is quite the case also for a country like South Korea.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What these countries' experiences suggest to us is that workplace norms, how accepting the co-workers and also the employers are for paternity leave utilisation, that is still something that is being worked on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the Singapore context, actually we have been making very good progress.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within the public sector, the utilisation rate is even higher, about 84%.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, within the public sector, the utilisation already surpasses some of the Nordic countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think a change of norms, which is something I see happening to a very large extent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You see very many more fathers are involved in the raising of their children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Can we encourage employers to be even more supportive?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is I think the fifth time the Member has asked the question about paternity leave in as many months.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we are happy to answer the Member's slightly different questions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope that the Member is equally happy with our slightly different answers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During the the Committee of Supply (COS) debate, where we get a chance to deal with marriage and parenthood in a more comprehensive manner, we can have a fuller exchange.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I seek the Member's indulgence for us to take the rest of his questions together in the COS debate.
